title: Given an array of positive numbers and a window size k, find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of exactly k elements. (GeeksforGeeks: Max Sum Subarray of size K)
shortTitle: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K (Fixed-Size Sliding Window)
keyPoints: Sum the first k elements to create the initial window, then slide by adding the new element and subtracting the old.
The sliding window reuses the previous sum, turning O(n*k) brute force into O(n) linear time.
The window size is fixed, so the logic is add-one-subtract-one per slide with no shrink condition.
An edge case is k larger than the array length, in which case no valid window exists.
This is distinct from the variable-size sliding window used in minimum-length or longest-substring problems.
The technique uses O(1) extra space beyond the input array.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sum the first window once, then slide by adding the new element and subtracting the old one, tracking the max.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Fixed-size sliding window** – a window of exactly k consecutive elements slides across the array one position at a time.
- **Sum update** – instead of recomputing from scratch, add the incoming element and subtract the outgoing element in O(1).
- **Maximum tracking** – compare the updated sum against the best seen so far after each slide.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
- **Precondition** – k must not exceed the array length; if it does, no valid window exists.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh wants to find the best k-day stretch of daily deposits, the window of exactly k consecutive days with the highest total. Instead of re-adding every k-day block from scratch, he keeps a running total for the current window, and each time he slides to the next day he adds the new day's deposit and drops the oldest day's deposit. He watches the running total and remembers the largest it ever reaches.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The maximum-sum-subarray-of-size-k problem is the textbook fixed-size sliding window. The brute-force computes every window from scratch, repeating most of the additions, but consecutive windows overlap in all but two elements, so you can update the running sum in constant time per slide.

You first add up the initial window of k elements and set it as both the running sum and the current maximum. Then you slide the window forward one position at a time: add the element entering on the right and subtract the element leaving on the left. After each slide, compare the running sum to the maximum and keep the larger. When the window reaches the end, the maximum holds the answer.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this on the analytics team. They reviewed a customer's daily deposit history and wanted to highlight the single best stretch of exactly k consecutive days, the window with the highest total inflow, for a marketing insight. The efficient sliding window with a reusable running sum kept the computation fast and memory-light.

The senior-level point is distinguishing the fixed-size window from the variable-size window. Here the window size never changes, so the logic is add-one-subtract-one per slide. In problems like smallest subarray with a given sum, the window grows and shrinks dynamically, which is a different pattern.

Remember one sentence: sum the first window, then slide by adding the new element and subtracting the old, tracking the maximum.
